Mechanics of hBN/ZnO vdW heteromaterials under tension
abstract: ABSTRACT Zinc oxide (ZnO) has been widely used as reinforcing fillers in rubber, paints, and ceramics due to its unique electrical properties, chemical stability, and low cost. However, its poor mechanical properties significantly restrict its reliability under long-term operation. As a two-dimensional nanomaterial, hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) has shown great potential for improving the mechanical properties of materials while simultaneously providing electrical insulation. This makes hBN a promising candidate for constructing hBN/ZnO van der Waals (vdW) heteromaterials to overcome the inherent shortcomings of ZnO, such as low stiffness, strength, and fracture resistance. In this study, we employed molecular dynamics (MD) simulations to explore the mechanical enhancement mechanism of ZnO in the form of vdW heterostructures through reinforcement with hBN under various strain rates, temperatures, hBN volume fractions ( V f ), and pressure. The tensile simulation results reveal that, at V f = 10%, ultimate stress (σ u ), fracture strain (ε f ), and Young's modulus ( E m ) increase by 21.2%, 34.0%, and 19.4%, respectively, compared to pure ZnO. These improvements arise from the load-bearing capacity of hBN, the optimization of the ZnO phase transition behavior during deformation and the interfacial coupling effect between hBN and ZnO. The findings further demonstrate that hBN can simultaneously improve the strength and toughness of ZnO, confirming ZnO/hBN vdW heterostructure as robust and reliable reinforcing fillers for high-performance non-metal composites.

title: Multi-modal vibration suppression using enhanced positive position feedback control
Compressive responses of ceramic lattices: Experiments and simulations
abstract: The strength of ceramic lattices is governed by their architecture, material defects, and geometrical imperfections. Most numerical models, however, incorporate only material defects or geometrical imperfections. Here, we introduce a modelling approach that combines both effects and is supported by experimental validation. Silica octet-truss lattices were fabricated by stereolithography with relative densities ranging from 9.5% to 33%. Computed tomography was used to quantify manufacturing imperfections, including non-uniform struts, material accumulation at the joints, and non-parallel surfaces. The scanned geometries were converted into finite element meshes, where each element was assigned a stochastic strength based on a Weibull distribution calibrated from separate tensile tests. The simulations successfully reproduced the progressive brittle fracture observed experimentally, including multiple load drops and the formation of a diagonal fracture plane. The results further showed that geometrical imperfections affect how the compressive strength scales with relative density, deviating from the expected stretching-dominated behavior. Overall, a very good agreement was obtained between experiments and simulations, demonstrating that accurately predicting the compressive response of ceramic lattices requires accounting for both geometrical imperfections and stochastic material strength.

title: Vibrational characteristics of star-shaped auxetic sandwich panels with openings
Thermal and cutting behaviour of Ti6Al4V in laser-assisted machining
Strength prediction with defect analysis of DLP-printed β-TCP scaffolds
abstract: Porous β -tricalcium phosphate ( β -TCP) scaffolds fabricated by digital light processing (DLP) are promising for load-bearing bone repair, yet their compressive strength remains difficult to predict because of intrinsic brittleness, architectural stress heterogeneity, and process-induced defects. Here, we establish a rapid, experimentally anchored framework for predicting the compressive strength of DLP-printed β -TCP scaffolds by coupling finite-element-derived stress heterogeneity with statistical strength characterization. Uniaxial compression tests on printed solid blocks confirm a Weibull strength distribution, which is used to assign local failure thresholds. Finite-element simulations of triply periodic minimal surface (TPMS) architectures provide stress-concentration-factor (SCF)–volume distributions that quantify geometry-induced stress amplification. By combining these inputs within a cumulative-damage criterion defined by a critical failed-volume fraction, scaffold-level strength is predicted using idealized geometries, with uncertainty estimated from repeated stochastic realizations. The framework is calibrated using 14 TPMS architectures and validated on non-calibrated porosity levels without additional fitting. The maximum principal stress yields the most accurate and rank-consistent predictions, and the predicted strengths are reported with 95% prediction intervals. Micro-computed tomography further shows that residual discrepancies are associated with architecture-dependent defect formation. A representative micro-CT-based finite-element analysis demonstrates that explicitly incorporating as-manufactured defects can substantially improve agreement with experiment, although at increased computational cost. Overall, the framework provides a practical first-order, geometry-based predictor for comparing relative strength levels across porous architectures, enabling rapid screening and defect-aware design of DLP-printed ceramic scaffolds.

title: Strain-rate-dependent model for elastic-plastic impacts
Nozzle-vibration piezoelectric jet for compact underwater robots
Uncovering size effects in crack compliance in nanobeams using MD simulations
abstract: The effect of a crack on the structural response of a nanobeam is commonly modeled by introducing a discontinuity in the slope at the cracked cross-section, with the magnitude proportional to the bending moment transmitted through the section. The proportionality factor (i.e., the crack compliance) is typically derived from closed-form solutions based on classical linear elastic fracture mechanics, whose validity at micro- and nanoscale dimensions is not well established. This study reveals size effects in the crack compliance of silicon nanobeams by integrating large-scale molecular dynamics (MD) simulations involving more than 2.3 million atoms with beam formulations derived from a local/nonlocal stress-driven gradient elasticity theory. Size-dependent bending and free transverse vibration responses of intact nanobeams are obtained through MD simulations and used to calibrate the nonlocal parameters of the continuum models. The calibrated models are then employed to study cracked nanobeams. Comparisons between MD predictions and theoretical results reveal pronounced size effects: classical formulas substantially underestimate crack-induced flexibility in nanobeams, while the discrepancy decreases with increasing beam length. We demonstrate that this size-dependent crack compliance is influenced by both the crystallographic orientation and the imposed boundary conditions. An atomic strain analysis reveals that the near-tip strain distribution in short nanobeams deviates from the classical singular form; however, for sufficiently long nanobeams (e.g., L ≈ 180 nm for a fixed–guided nanobeam under bending), discrete atomic effects become negligible, and strain distribution and crack compliance converge toward classical predictions.

title: Enhanced flexoelectric metamaterials through chiral curved ligaments design
Thermally driven reusable dual-phase honeycombs with enhanced mechanical properties
abstract: This work develops dual-phase honeycombs combining a hyperelastic soft material phase (thermoplastic polyurethane, TPU) and an elastoplastic hard material phase (polylactic acid, PLA) to balance mechanical performance and reusability. Encasing the hard phase within the soft phase leverages PLA’s shape memory and TPU’s shape recovery to enhance energy dissipation, shape recovery, and structural robustness. Fabricated via fused deposition modeling, the design was tested under quasi-static compression across various tessellations (periodic square, hexagonal, triangular, and aperiodic hat). At 60 °C thermal recovery, the structure restored 98.8% of its original height on average. Higher hard phase content improved mechanical performance but reduced reusability. Hexagonal tiling showed superior energy absorption and cyclic stability, while square and triangular designs optimized stiffness and strength. Heat treatment at 160 °C (PLA’s melting point) further enhanced plateau stress and recovery. This dual-phase design offers a reusable solution for applications like sports helmets, knee pads, and packaging, achieving a synergistic balance of mechanical robustness and reusability through tailored phase composition and geometry.

title: Vacuum-driven robotic grippers with reliable and powerful grasping capability
Geometry-driven programmable actuation of a Kresling origami soft robotic arm
Iso-energetic ballistic response of meso-scale woven fabrics
Stochastic lattice modeling of correlated graphene disorder
abstract: Nanoscale disorder in graphene is commonly modeled as spatially uncorrelated variability of interatomic parameters, although atomistic fluctuations and microstructural effects often exhibit spatial organization over finite length scales. The influence of such spatial correlation on the apparent mechanical response of graphene remains largely unexplored. This work introduces a novel stochastic lattice mechanics framework in which the correlation length of interatomic variability is treated as an explicit control parameter governing the elastic response of finite graphene sheets. Bond stretching and angular stiffness parameters are modeled as spatially correlated random fields with physically bounded marginal distributions, enabling systematic uncertainty propagation from the lattice scale to apparent elastic properties. Virtual uniaxial tensile tests along the zigzag and armchair directions are performed to evaluate directional Young’s moduli and Poisson’s ratios. The results show that spatial correlation affects not only the dispersion of elastic properties but also their mean values. Increasing correlation length produces correlation-induced stiffening and amplifies elastic anisotropy by promoting spatially coherent load-bearing regions and reducing microscopic self-averaging. Spatial correlation additionally alters the coupling between axial stiffness and transverse deformation, leading to systematic shifts and increased variability of Poisson’s ratios. These findings identify correlation length as a higher-order parameter governing the apparent elastic behavior of graphene and establish spatial organization of nanoscale disorder as a mechanically significant mechanism in two-dimensional lattice materials. The proposed framework provides a computationally efficient tool for stochastic graphene analysis and lattice-based modeling of materials with spatially structured nanoscale disorder.

title: Microstructure control and nanoengineering reinforcement of additively manufactured TiO2/ZrO2-Al2O3 ceramics
A multi-phase multi-physics phase-field model for autogenous shrinkage of concrete
Programming energy absorption via 4D-printed reconfigurable gradient metamaterials
Spectral contact networks for granular base load spreading
abstract: Unbound granular bases redistribute traffic loads through heterogeneous particle contacts, but pavement-scale analyses rarely provide a lightweight operator linking contact-network structure to transmitted base-reaction footprints. This study proposes a spectral contact-network surrogate for moving-load transfer in granular base layers. A compacted assembly is mapped to a stiffness-weighted contact graph, and an energy-based reduction under vertical kinematics yields a sparse grounded Laplacian system coupling internal contact transmission with subgrade support. The operator directly outputs reaction footprints and spreading metrics while retaining interpretation in terms of contact topology, stiffness heterogeneity, and spectral bottlenecks. Moving loads are represented by repeated quasi-static solves along the top boundary to generate footprint maps, peak reactions, spreading widths, localization metrics, and entropy-based dispersion indicators. Spectral diagnostics identify weak partitions and connectivity-critical edges, while proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) shows that the footprint evolution is strongly low-rank, with approximately five modes capturing 90% of the footprint energy and six modes capturing 95%. Comparison with discrete element method (DEM) simulations for localized compaction shows that the framework captures the dominant directional kinematic signature. Computationally, each DEM case required about 20 min, whereas the proposed framework completed the corresponding case in less than 10 s after assembling the contact graph and grounded system. The results show that load spreading is governed jointly by contact-network redundancy, support constraint, and load position, and that targeted removal of connectivity-critical edges causes stronger deterioration than random damage. The framework provides an efficient and interpretable intermediate-scale tool for granular load-transfer analysis beyond homogenized continuum descriptors.

title: Particle-damping-enhanced inertial amplification metamaterials for low and broadband vibration attenuation
Modular discrete mechanical metamaterials: Structural classification, design strategies and mechanical responses
Snap-through of soft elliptical shells under volume- and pressure-control
abstract: Soft materials are widely used in engineering applications due to their flexibility, energy absorption capability, and low prototyping cost. These characteristics make such materials an ideal basis for designing complex, compliant mechanical systems, addressed in soft robotics. Additionally, they often exhibit significant material and structural nonlinearities, which can be exploited through snap-through instability to achieve rapid and enhanced mechanical responses. While snap-through behavior has been extensively studied in the literature for soft spherical shells, this contribution extends shell geometries considering an axisymmetric elliptical generalization using fluidic actuation. A comprehensive framework is proposed for capturing the snap-through behavior of soft axisymmetric elliptical shells through numerical and experimental methods, utilizing volume- and pressure-controlled methods. A general geometric formulation is introduced to describe elliptical shells, and finite element models are developed to analyze their nonlinear snapping behavior. The numerical results are validated using a dedicated experimental setup capable of reproducing both control methods. The results show that axisymmetric simulations provide an efficient and reliable tool for parameter studies, while dynamic 3D simulations closely follow the stable branches of the quasi-static equilibrium paths. Equivalent energy-release geometries are identified, revealing a linear relation between key geometric parameters that enables the structural response to be tuned without changing the overall actuator size. The experiments confirm that volume control provides a more robust characterization of snap-through, whereas pressure control is more sensitive to control-loop limitations. Overall, the results demonstrate that elliptical shells offer additional geometric flexibility while preserving the performance of spherical snap-through actuators.

abstract: Finite element quasi-static analyses of deformation to failure in a shear specimen are carried out based on a finite deformation elasto-viscoplastic formulation incorporating ductile damage progression. Multisurface porous material plasticity constitutive relations, termed HUNNY, are employed which account for the evolution of microvoids under arbitrary loading. Complete loss of traction carrying capacity at the material point level occurs when porosity within a finite-thickness band approaches unity, thereby leading to final material failure by coalescence of crack-like voids. In the present analyses, the material is assumed to have pre-existing voids. Within regions of intense shear, the voids elongate and rotate, leading to an increase in band porosity and hence to the formation of a macroscopic crack, unless void closure occurs prior to coalescence. The increase in band porosity is generally accompanied with a decrease in total porosity, yet not precluding coalescence. The phenomenology of cracking in the shear specimen, as predicted by the constitutive HUNNY theory for a specific set of initial microstructural parameters, is described in some detail. Depending on the initial distribution of voids, one or more cracks initiate either in the bulk and propagate outward to the surface or at the surface and propagate inward, eventually leading to severance of the specimen. These two crack progression modes are qualitatively consistent with experimental observations. Crack initiation in the bulk is found to be associated with the “knee” of the macroscopic force–displacement curve, whereas surface initiation is not. Ultimately, the propagation of cracks leads to a complete drop in the load carrying capacity of the specimen.

abstract: Additively manufactured foamed PLA is a promising material for sandwich cores thanks to its adjustable density and mechanical properties. However, the manufacturing process shows high variability and complexity, so a systematic method is needed to control porosity while maintaining a consistent metastructure and ensuring low variability in mechanical performance. This study introduces a manufacturing approach that achieves tailored part densities and a uniform metastructure by primarily adjusting the flow rate. The hot-end temperature is only modified at the density limits. Tensile tests and four-point bending tests on sandwich structures, combined with Digital Image Correlation, are performed for a comprehensive characterization of the elastic properties across multiple PLA foam densities and 3D-printed infill angles. The results are consistent, demonstrating a strong dependence of material properties on density and revealing anisotropic behavior, particularly at higher densities. Finally, the characterization methodology and the estimated mechanical properties are validated by finite element model calculations of the four-point bending tests. This work provides a comprehensive framework to design and manufacture functionally graded 3D-printed foamed PLA structures with tailored mechanical properties and performance.

abstract: Accurate characterisation of tool-chip contact in metal cutting is essential for understanding tool wear and surface integrity, particularly in critical applications where tight tolerances and high quality are required. However, capturing friction behaviour under realistic cutting conditions remains challenging, especially for difficult-to-cut alloys that generate severe thermomechanical loads. This paper presents an optimised Partially Restricted Contact Length Tool (PRCLT) methodology for characterising tool-chip friction. The methodology is applied for the first time to machining Udimet 720 Li, a next-generation aerospace nickel-based alloy, using T15 High-Speed Steel tools under broaching conditions at cutting speeds of 2.5–7.5 m·min −1 and feeds of 0.05–0.15 mm. The optimised PRCLT design provided reliable, high-resolution mapping of normal and friction stresses along the rake face, with errors below 3%. The results confirm a sticking-sliding friction model: near the cutting edge, friction stress is limited by the shear flow stress of the workpiece material, while further along the rake face the contact transitions to Coulomb friction with a coefficient of 1.3–1.4. These findings demonstrate the robustness of the PRCLT method for characterising tool-chip contact in difficult-to-cut alloys.

abstract: Accurate aerodynamic damping quantification is essential for aeroelastic stability analysis and controller design of floating offshore wind turbines (FOWTs). To facilitate quantifying aerodynamic damping of different modes of FOWT accounting for full aeroelastic coupling, an analytical modeling framework is proposed to extract the full degree-of-freedom (DOF) aerodynamic damping matrix. A 17-DOF aero-hydro-servo-elastic dynamic model is first established and verified against OpenFAST results under both steady-state and transient operating conditions. By employing a multi-step Taylor series expansion, the blade velocities and aerodynamic loads are analytically linearized, enabling explicit closed-form expressions of aerodynamic damping coefficients as well as formulation of a pitch vector that is needed in the servo-controller of the linearized FOWT model. Based on the proposed framework, a systematic investigation is conducted to quantify multi-mode aerodynamic damping ratios of FOWT while accounting for key modeling aspects, including tower-top rotation, blade pitch angle, and turbine–platform coupling. The results indicate that tower-top rotation plays a crucial role in aerodynamic coupling between tower fore–aft motion and the sway, heave, and yaw DOFs of floating platforms. In addition, neglecting blade pitch angle leads to significant overestimation of aerodynamic damping for edgewise whirling modes. The proposed modeling framework provides closed-form, fully-coupled aerodynamic damping matrix for FOWTs at arbitrary operating points without reliance on numerical perturbation or fitting procedures, offering an accurate and efficient tool for aeroelastic stability analysis. The analytically derived aerodynamic coefficients can be readily integrated into decoupled platform finite element and frequency-domain models, enabling preliminary floating-platform design and rapid concept selection.

abstract: Additively manufactured lattice metamaterials provide exceptional strength-to-weight ratios, yet their mechanical properties critically depend on specimen size. A core design challenge is therefore defining a minimum representative volume—the smallest cell array that yields bulklike, size-invariant properties—to ensure reliable performance. While often discussed, this critical scale has never been rigorously established for architected lattices. Here, through integrated experiments and numerical simulations on metallic (AlSi10Mg) and polymeric (ABS) lattices spanning multiple topologies (simple cubic, body-centred cubic, and octet-truss) and a broad range of strut slenderness ratios, encompassing bending-dominated, stretching-dominated, and transitional deformation regimes, we establish the first systematic general convergence criterion. We show that a 5 × 5 × 5 cell array ensures convergence of elastic modulus and strength, independent of topology, material, or absolute scale. Crucially, while this threshold is general, it is found that the deformation regime plays a previously unreported role in governing the pathway to convergence as array size increases. Stretching-dominated architectures converge earlier than bending-dominated ones, and lattices exhibiting simultaneous bending, stretching, and shear achieve the earliest convergence of all. Across deformation regimes, strength stabilizes prior to modulus and failure modes evolving from boundary-driven collapse to progressive, bulk-like failure. These material-independent design rules eliminate the need for exhaustive size-scaling studies, accelerating the development of reliable lightweight lattice metamaterials for advanced engineering applications.

Automated design of tubular origami with anisotropic stiffness
abstract: Thin sheets can be assembled into tubular origami structures that combine deployability with pronounced anisotropic stiffness, enabling applications ranging from robotics to deployable systems. However, most existing tubular origami designs remain limited to degree-four vertex and are characterized primarily in axial and radial loading modes, without a full assessment of anisotropic stiffness. Here, we present an automated design scheme for tubular origami that jointly explores local vertex topology through generalized degree- n vertices and global tube topology through its polygonal cross-section, for the systematic design and optimization of anisotropic stiffness. Using a calibrated bar-and-hinge model together with experimental validation, we quantify large-deformation stiffness responses in axial translation, in-plane translation, torsion about the tube axis, and rotation about in-plane axes, thereby characterizing the anisotropic stiffness of the tube across its compliant and constrained deformation modes. The resulting design-space exploration showed that the polygonal cross-sectional topology and its associated geometry jointly govern the anisotropic stiffness. We further show that increasing the local vertex degree can improve global structural performance, particularly for tubes with a small number of cross-sectional vertices, demonstrating that higher local kinematic freedom does not necessarily compromise stiffness at the structural scale. Together, these results highlight local origami vertex degree and polygonal cross-sectional geometry as powerful design variables for tailoring anisotropic stiffness in tubular origami.

title: Moving-boundary elastica predicts looped-end braided stent crimping
abstract: Looped-ended braided stents are used in vascular interventions owing to their flexibility, conformability, and self-expansion. However, severe crimping into low-profile delivery catheters concentrates bending, crossing-point migration, and geometric crowding at the terminal crowns, producing stresses that classical uniform-braid models cannot resolve. This limitation is critical for bioabsorbable metallic stents, where excessive end-region stress may compromise deliverability or exceed yield limits. To address this gap, this study develops a large-deformation moving-boundary elastica model that represents the terminal crown as a planar elastica with a moving crossing point and predicts maximum bending stress, radial force, and local geometric jamming. The model was verified against finite element simulations spanning stiffness, pitch angle, wire diameter, loop radius, wire number, and stent diameter, and compared with experimental crimping data for a looped-ended Nitinol braided stent. The predictions showed close agreement with finite element stress and radial-force responses throughout the planar sliding regime and followed the measured force trend before stress-induced martensitic transformation. In high-wire-density configurations, deviations marked the transition to out-of-plane crown buckling and defined the planar model limit. The results establish the looped end as a design-limiting region and provide an end-specific framework for rapid loop-end screening before finite element analysis or prototype testing

abstract: Elastic wave mode conversion is essential for wave manipulation and non-destructive evaluation, yet transverse waves remain more difficult to excite than longitudinal waves. This work proposes an elastic metasurface for high-efficiency longitudinal-to-transverse (L-T) mode conversion, designed using an explicit parametric topology optimization method based on movable elliptic voids (MEV). In this approach, the topological configuration of the metasurface is explicitly described by a set of movable elliptic voids and mapped onto a fixed grid region. Theory of transmission with mode conversion is developed and the mode conversion efficiency is defined for the optimal design of the unitcell. Numerical analyses are then performed to investigate the mode conversion mechanism, impedance characteristics, robustness, and bandwidth of the unitcells. The results show that different optimized unitcells exhibit either frequency-selective or frequency-tolerant responses, indicating the potential for multifunctional design. The mode conversion metasurfaces are constructed for full wave field numerical simulations and experimental verifications. The results demonstrate that L-T mode conversion can be achieved with high efficiency at the target frequency. This study provides an efficient design strategy for elastic metasurfaces enabling mode conversion, with potential applications in non-destructive testing.

abstract: Crystallographic texture in polycrystalline materials, such as in Hexagonal Close-Packed metals, strongly influences their mechanical and physical performance. Texture commonly develops during thermomechanical deformations that engineering metal components undergo during manufacturing, yet accurate bulk texture characterisation remains challenging, especially in components with curved geometries. This paper introduces a non-destructive ultrasonic methodology that combines Green’s function reconstruction from diffuse wave fields with ultrasonic texture inversion to enable volumetric texture characterisation in such components. Finite element simulations were employed to investigate and optimise the diffuse field generation process, assessing different phased array excitation strategies, including non-steered, beam-steered, and phase-shifted modes, with emphasis on improving the reconstruction accuracy of the longitudinal wave component. Directional wave velocities extracted from the reconstructed Green’s functions were processed using an established ultrasonic texture inversion framework to determine the bulk crystallographic texture. The reconstructed texture shows strong agreement with Electron Backscatter Diffraction measurements, demonstrating the accuracy of the proposed approach. The presented methodology extends ultrasonic bulk texture characterisation to curved components and broadens the applicability of ultrasonic techniques for non-destructive evaluation in engineering applications.

abstract: Accurate characterisation of complex residual stress requires resolving underlying inelastic strains, which often exhibit unobservable or discontinuous features. This study establishes the fundamental identifiability limits of eigenstrain tomography when mapping sparse diffraction measurements to volumetric discontinuous and impotent (stress-free null) strain states. The results demonstrate that the mechanics-informed inversion intrinsically isolates unobservable impotent modes without artificial mathematical smoothing, provided the acquisition path is geometrically complete. The key novelty lies in identifying a strict dimensional threshold for triaxial deformation. While uniaxial states are uniquely identifiable from single-component data, resolving fully triaxial fields inherently requires multi-component, orthogonal strain measurements to decouple structural cross-talk. This dimensional threshold advances the fundamental theory of ill-posed inverse problems in continuum mechanics by redefining data sufficiency requirements for multi-axial reconstruction. These findings provide mechanics-based observability criteria for experimental design, proving that sharp resolution of embedded boundaries is fundamentally limited by tomographic acquisition completeness.

abstract: The dynamics of a composite laminate conical shell is analysed in this paper. The conical geometry of the shell, combined with a tailored laminate layout, is proposed to create a bistable structure which, after clamping, exhibits two stable equilibrium configurations, I-shape and C-shape. Finite elements (FE) modeling and experimental tests performed on manufactured prototypes reveal both local (in-well) and global (cross-well) dynamic responses. The influence of the shell’s cantilever length on the snap-through behaviour is investigated and then an active element is embedded to bistable shell to harvest energy from in-well and cross-well oscillations. Based on the FE model and experimental results, a reduced-order model of the active system is developed. It is shown that two different mechanisms lead to snap-through transitions between the I and C configurations, significantly affecting the global dynamics of the shell. The generated voltage levels are reported for various initial conditions, excitation amplitudes and frequencies, and possible interactions between I–C modes are discussed.

title: Directional deformation prediction of strut-based lattices via Gauss map embedding
abstract: This paper aims to develop an efficient and topology-agnostic framework for predicting direction-dependent mechanical responses of strut-based lattice materials. A Gaussian sphere (GS)-based representation is introduced, in which strut orientations and node positions are mapped onto discretized Gauss maps to jointly encode load-bearing directions, strut weighting, and nodal topology. A dataset of 28 cubic lattice architectures sampled over 380 loading orientations was generated using finite element analysis (FEA), where directional deformation served as the learning target. The originality of the work lies in replacing topology-specific graph or homogenization-based descriptions with a compact orientation-space embedding that explicitly preserves anisotropic geometric features. The proposed Gauss-map model achieved accurate directional deformation prediction with an overall MAE of 0.0220 mm and a 2232 × inference speedup over a tuned Message Passing Neural Networks baseline, while maintaining comparable held-out test performance. Experimental validation using rotated Octet-truss specimens further showed that FEA agrees more closely with measured directional modulus responses than homogenization, with MAEs of 0.56 MPa and 6.26 MPa, respectively. These findings demonstrate that GS-based embeddings provide a physically meaningful and computationally efficient descriptor for learning anisotropic lattice behavior, with practical implications for rapid lattice screening, inverse design, and optimization of directionally tailored architected materials.

Confinement and granular cohesion govern self-propelled intruder ascent
abstract: Self-propelled ascent in wet granular media remains poorly understood because cohesion, local fluidization, and geometric confinement are strongly coupled. Existing studies have mainly considered self-propelled intruders in dry granular beds or passive segregation under externally imposed flow. The central contribution of this work is an active-region framework that links liquid-bridge cohesion and finite-width confinement to local granular flow and intruder mobility. Experiments and calibrated discrete element simulations of a self-propelled spherical intruder reveal an initial quasi-static rising regime followed by a dynamic regime. Hydrostatic loading and liquid-bridge cohesion dominate the former, whereas developed local fluidization and inertial effects govern the latter. Wet cohesion stabilizes the particle network and suppresses the formation and expansion of the dynamically active region, thereby reducing the rising velocity. Narrow containers similarly restrict lateral grain rearrangement through wall-mediated force-chain transmission, while this confinement effect becomes negligible beyond a critical width. Variation of the intruder-to-particle size ratio reveals a non-monotonic response and a driving-dependent critical size ratio, R c . Below R c , increasing the size ratio expands the active region and accelerates ascent; above R c , the active-region extent approaches saturation and geometric confinement inhibits further ascent. Incorporating this crossover into an inertial-number relation yields a size-corrected scaling law for the rising velocity. These results provide a unified mechanistic and quantitative description of how cohesion and confinement regulate self-propelled transport through granular media.

abstract: Conceptual models of a rotary nonlinear vibration absorber incorporating either a magnet mass–spring oscillator placed inside a solenoid or a piezoelectric element in series with a regular mass–spring oscillator are considered. Both assemblages can simultaneously mitigate the vibration of a rigid cylinder subjected to parametric excitation, and harvest energy. Mechanical impacts between the inner oscillator mass and the cylinder’s internal wall are implicitly accounted for. The study builds on previous work in which the piezoelectric element was coupled to the rotary nonlinear vibration absorber. It highlights the development of a self-tuning rotary nonlinear vibration absorber integrated with a mechanical impact oscillator. It provides a direct performance comparison between the two assemblages across several scenarios and over a range of relevant system parameters through numerical analysis, complemented with qualitative case studies of the magneto-electromechanical system. Using advanced analytical tools such as Poincaré maps, Floquet theory, orbit diagrams, and recurrence plots, the study delivers a comprehensive characterisation of the system’s dynamic behaviour.

abstract: Full-field three-dimensional residual stress assessment in additively manufactured components remains a critical challenge in solid mechanics, owing to the complex nature of internal stress fields, limited experimental accessibility, and the high computational cost of transient thermomechanical simulations. To overcome this limitation, this study introduces a stable, physics-constrained inverse framework utilising sparse-projection eigenstrain tomography to assess a cubic laser powder bed fusion AlSi10Mg test specimen. While conventional synchrotron mapping requires days of acquisition, the proposed approach reconstructs voxel-parameterised incompatible strain fields and recovers the full six-component residual stress tensor from only two orthogonal projections. By mathematically embedding the continuum mechanics constraints of macroscopic force equilibrium and Saint-Venant strain compatibility, the fundamentally ill-posed inverse problem is rendered numerically stable. This work represents the successful full-tensor volumetric reconstruction from sparse projections in an additively manufactured component. This novel experimental reconstruction provides a rigorous physical dataset, which is evaluated against a transient non-linear thermomechanical finite element model. Both routes exhibit robust morphological agreement in reproducing the characteristic compressive interior and tensile vertical edges of the part. This qualitative validation reveals a critical physical distinction where the numerical model provides the idealised macroscopic continuum baseline, while the inverse tomography simultaneously captures and preserves sharp, localised micro-mechanical variations. By reducing the number of projections for volumetric evaluation, this framework provides a highly efficient and mathematically rigorous tool for complex residual stress analysis.

abstract: This study proposes an experiment-efficient ANN-based framework for characterizing the anisotropy of AA6022-T4 and calibrating the Yld2004-18p anisotropic yield function from a single hole expansion (HE) test and evaluates its predictions against two texture-driven meso-scale plasticity approaches, namely crystal plasticity finite element method (CPFEM) and elasto-visco-plastic self-consistent (ΔEVPSC). The ANN framework exploits the heterogeneous deformation field generated during the HE test, with training data obtained from finite element (FE) simulations using randomly assigned Yld2004-18p parameters. Two distinct ANN frameworks are developed: one predicts anisotropic properties (stress ratios and r-values), while the other directly estimates Yld2004-18p parameters. Three ANN input selection strategies are explored, i.e., using all strain components from 21 extraction locations in the HE simulation, local stress-based selection, and a variance-based approach. In the crystal plasticity approaches, CPFEM and ΔEVPSC simulations based solely on the measured initial crystallographic texture provide virtual uniaxial and equibiaxial responses that are subsequently fitted to Yld2004-18p. Comparative assessment shows that the ANN framework, as well as the CPFEM- and ΔEVPSC-based approaches, reproduces the anisotropic response, yield locus, and HE thinning profile of the material with generally good agreement with experiments and with the conventional calibration, while substantially reducing experimental time, cost, and material consumption.

abstract: Two-dimensional (2D) lattice metamaterials are widely used as lightweight cores, impact energy absorbers, and load-bearing cellular structures in aerospace, transportation, and civil engineering applications. This study presents a novel and comprehensive design approach aimed at improving mechanical properties in 2D reentrant metamaterials, including in-plane/out-of-plane energy absorption with stable deformation patterns. The proposed concept reformulates the conventional straight extrusion path with a zigzag configuration in reentrant metamaterials, which can also be applied to any 2D metamaterials via a fused deposition modelling (FDM) three-dimensional (3D) printer, while keeping the mass and overall dimensions of all structures constant. From the solid-mechanics standpoint, by transforming the traditional rectangular cross-section into a parallelogram shape by an inclination angle of “θ”, the product of inertia that measures how an area is distributed simultaneously about two perpendicular axes is introduced. This leads to tilting the neutral axis of each inclined segment and stress imbalance within each segment. Once the segments with different inclination angles are stacked and compressed, high-stiffness and stress regions appear at the interfaces of two adjacent inclined segments, resulting in redistributed bending of the cell walls and high energy absorption. Finite element analysis (FEA), analytical modelling, and experimentally validated results obtained from TPU-based reentrant metamaterials support tunable mechanical properties such as stiffness variation across a wide range, from soft to rigid. As an example, considering TPU as a hyperelastic material showing highly non-linear behavior, zigzag-based metamaterials can exhibit a variety of structural behavior, ranging from linear to semi-elastoplastic under compression. Under in-plane compression, machine learning regression, Gaussian process regression (GPR), was further applied to fifty-six metamaterials with two input features of “inclination angle” and “depth” to generate heatmaps correlating specific energy absorption (SEA) and structural stiffness dependency on input features. Under out-of-plane compression, the zigzag arrangement effectively redistributes strain and stress across interfaces, leading to an increase in the critical buckling load, and providing better stability due to strain redistribution under compression. In the end, to demonstrate the comprehensiveness and reliability of the proposed design approach, the in-plane/out-of-plane properties of the zigzag-based honeycomb are compared with those of traditional straight extrusion honeycomb as a case study, supporting the applicability of the proposed design approach to any 2D metamaterial.

abstract: Hierarchical nanoporous metals infiltrated with polymers offer enhanced tensile stability while retaining functional porosity, yet their micromechanical deformation mechanisms remain insufficiently understood. Here, a micromechanics-based finite element framework is developed for epoxy-filled hierarchical nanoporous copper (HNPCu) based on experimentally derived structural parameters. The hierarchical ligament architecture across two structural levels as well as selective epoxy infiltration are explicitly resolved, enabling phase-specific analysis of local stress and strain evolution. The predicted tensile response is validated against experiments for different Cu solid fractions ( 0.1 ≤ φ ≤ 0.2 ), and the experimentally observed trends are well reproduced using idealized microstructures. Epoxy infiltration markedly reduces plastic strain localization within the Cu network, leading to a more homogeneous deformation state compared to epoxy-free HNPCu. At the macroscopic level, the tensile response remains largely unaffected by epoxy infiltration at small strains, with differences emerging only at larger deformation. Strain localization is predicted both within Cu ligaments and near Cu–epoxy interfaces, consistent with experimentally observed microcrack formation along phase boundaries and inside the Cu network. These findings provide micromechanical insight into hierarchy-assisted deformation in polymer-infiltrated nanoporous metals and establish a basis for microstructure-guided design of mechanically robust hierarchical materials.

Explicit nonlocal Lemaitre damage for dynamic ductile fracture
abstract: Dynamic ductile fracture in metallic structures involves large deformation, strain localization, crack initiation, and progressive material separation, making mesh-objective simulation difficult. In explicit finite element analyses, local damage models combined with element deletion may produce mesh-dependent crack paths and energy dissipation. This study develops an explicit nonlocal Lemaitre damage framework in which integral-type Gaussian averaging is coupled with an objective large-deformation Kirchhoff stress update. The coupled nonlocal constitutive problem is integrated without using a preceding-step proportional-factor approximation. Final material separation is controlled by a local equivalent-plastic-strain threshold numerically derived from reference local damage simulations rather than by the spatially averaged damage variable, thereby separating constitutive regularization from element removal and avoiding discontinuous failed regions and artificial residual ligaments. The underlying elastoplastic damage formulation is validated against tensile tests of DC04 steel up to fracture initiation, showing good agreement with the measured force–displacement response and necking-zone thickness reduction. Tensile mesh-sensitivity analyses produce smoother damage fields and more consistent post-peak responses than the local model. For the single-edge-notched plate, the mesh-induced variation in work to failure decreases from 40.38% to 10.14%, while the variations in peak force, peak displacement, and failure displacement decrease to 0.54%, 2.96%, and 2.30%, respectively. Perforated-plate simulations further demonstrate ligament-controlled crack coalescence and loading-direction-dependent fracture patterns. Energy histories remain bounded during damage evolution and element deletion, with negligible artificial energy and no mass scaling. The proposed framework provides a practical and less mesh-sensitive approach for explicit dynamic ductile-fracture simulation.

Hypervelocity impact response of 3D-printed metallic space fabric shields
abstract: The pursuit of large orbital platforms and crewed spacecraft has intensified the need for lightweight, deployable shielding systems against micrometeoroid and orbital debris (MMOD) impacts. Inflatable habitats are a promising solution, but the fabric-based shields conventionally used for such structures provide inferior protection compared with metallic bumpers because of their low shock impedance and are vulnerable to atomic oxygen erosion in orbit. To address these limitations, a 3D-printed metallic chainmail-based space fabric is proposed as a flexible metallic bumper for micrometeoroid and orbital debris protection: a structure that folds like a fabric yet retains the shock impedance of solid metal, and whose hypervelocity impact response has not previously been characterized. Smoothed particle hydrodynamics simulations identify local mass discontinuities between chainmail unit cells as the primary source of this vulnerability, motivating the development of tilted metallic space fabric geometry that reorients the unit-cell elements to redistribute the projected mass and suppress these discontinuities. The optimized structure was fabricated by metal additive manufacturing and evaluated using two-stage light gas gun impact tests. The tilted metallic space fabric generated an anisotropic debris cloud and achieved a lower rear-wall maximum penetration depth than Nextel AF62 fabric despite its lower areal density. Additional simulations under the experimental impact conditions reproduced the observed debris-cloud morphology and rear-wall damage pattern with good agreement. These results establish the tilted metallic space fabric as a novel, flexible metallic shielding concept for future inflatable space structures.

Tribo-dynamics of coupled multi-clearance diesel engine bearings under dynamic misalignment
abstract: Crankshaft tilt misalignment alters the load-transfer path in the diesel engine crank–connecting-rod mechanism, whereas the tribo-dynamics of coupled multi-clearance bearings with dynamically varying local misalignment remain less understood. This study investigates the connecting-rod big-end bearing (CRBEB), connecting-rod small-end bearing (CRSEB), and bilateral piston-pin boss bearings (PPBBs) as coupled multi-clearance bearings under crankshaft tilt. A multi-clearance tribo-dynamic model is developed by coupling Lagrange-equation-based multibody dynamics, transient mixed lubrication, and an asperity contact model. The formulation retains the rocking degrees of freedom of the connecting rod and piston pin, and further captures the dynamic journal–bearing misalignment within the bearing clearances induced by their posture evolution. On this basis, the propagation of dynamic misalignment and the mechanism of load redistribution in multi-clearance bearings under crankshaft tilt are elucidated. The results show that crankshaft tilt causes synchronous rod-pin rocking and asymmetric load redistribution toward the tilted-side PPBB, leading to higher oil-film pressure and asperity contact in the tilted-side end-face region. Compared with the single-clearance model, the additional compliant load-transfer paths provided by the CRSEB and PPBBs alleviate local load concentration in the CRBEB. However, increasing crankshaft tilt angle or CRBEB radial clearance still aggravates asymmetric lubrication and rocking response within the multi-clearance model. Wear analysis and engine tests show consistent upper-shell end-face damage tendency and enhanced high-frequency vibration impacts under worn conditions. This study provides mechanistic support for interpreting tribo-dynamic responses and bearing shell fault signatures in coupled multi-clearance bearings in diesel engines.

Image-based modelling of rock non-linear deformation under low stress levels
abstract: This study presents an image-based method for simulating the non-linear deformation of rocks caused by the pore-closure effect under increasing confining stress, by incorporating the partial-volume effect inherent in low-resolution digital rock images. The method first reconstructs digital rock models in which each voxel is assigned a pore fraction value between 0 and 1. Each partial-volume voxel is then treated as a two-part spring, where the compliant pore phase deforms before the stiffer solid phase. The continuous non-linear deformation process is discretised into a sequence of linear finite-element steps, each driven by a fixed macroscopic strain. The predictions of the method agree well with experimental stress–strain curves and wave velocities measured on three sandstone samples. These results demonstrate that the proposed method not only captures the macroscopic non-linear deformation but also provides direct pore-scale insight into the microstructural evolution that governs the mechanical behaviour of rocks under confinement.

High-frequency inertial control approach for ultra-precision machine dynamic stiffness enhancement
abstract: Vibration control remains challenging in ultra-precision machine tools, where compact architectures and stringent motion-accuracy requirements limit conventional damping solutions. Beyond conventional energy-dissipative damping methods, this paper proposes a high-frequency inertial control approach that applies controlled harmonic excitation directly to the stage carriage. As inertial effects become dominant, the resulting inertial interaction increases effective dynamic stiffness, reduces structural receptance, and suppresses vibration. We systematically model actuation-induced disturbances at the pressurised air film interface to capture the coupled dynamics while preserving motion accuracy. Model-guided design identifies an optimal actuator-source dynamic transmission path, yielding near-ideal system behaviour and a consistent reduction in vibration acceleration under near non-dissipative air film conditions. Experimental machining tests show that, at 600 Hz, the proposed approach markedly suppresses chatter. Specifically, the surface roughness Sa decreases from 0.298 to 0.224 μm, while cutting-force fluctuations decrease from 8.15 to 5.53 N, accompanied by reduced grain-impact-induced subsurface crack propagation. More broadly, this work establishes high-frequency inertial control as a structurally integrated strategy for regulating machine dynamics, providing a practical route towards vibration-resilient precision machine tools.

title: Nonideality of simple shear deformation and shear strain assessment
abstract: The study of simple shear (or simple shear dominated) deformation has garnered increasing attention, as it can be leveraged either to design novel materials and structures (e.g., metamaterials and wearable sensor arrays) or to characterize the mechanical behaviors of materials (e.g., metallic materials, composite materials and emerging soft materials). In these scenarios, shear strain is a widely used metric for measuring deformation, making the accurate assessment of shear strain an important problem. However, existing methods for assessing shear strain are varied and often overlook the nonideality of simple shear, which can involve a combination of simple shear, rotation & normal strain - a complexity commonly encountered in real-world scenarios. This oversight can lead to errors and the implications of this issue has not been well understood. This study presents a novel, unified shear kinematics for describing the nonideality of simple shear, which is then leveraged to conduct a comprehensive analytical and numerical investigation into the influence of nonideality on shear strain assessment. The results demonstrate that existing methods for evaluating shear strain are inadequate to, and there may be no method fully applicable to the most challenging cases of non-ideal simple shear deformation. This study further proposes two novel shear strain assessment methods to overcome these limitations. Additionally, experimental studies are conducted to validate the newly proposed kinematics and shear strain assessment method. Practical guidelines for selecting simple shear assessment method are also presented. The outcomes of this research are anticipated to advance the understanding of simple shear deformation in real-world scenarios, leading to more accurate shear strain assessments in the field of mechanics, material science and manufacturing.

Global form-to-performance trimming of hemispherical resonators
abstract: The dynamic performance of hemispherical resonator gyroscopes is governed by the mass and stiffness uniformity of the hemispherical resonator. Conventional performance-based trimming cannot simultaneously decouple the 1st to 4th harmonic errors, and trimming low-order harmonics inevitably introduces higher-order ones. To overcome the limitation, this paper proposes a global form-to-performance trimming method that converts measured 3D form errors into a removal distribution, suppressing the 1st to 4th harmonic errors synchronously without performance feedback. Firstly, an analytical model is established, revealing the quantitative relationships of frequency split and anchor loss to the inner and outer surface form errors. Secondly, an objective function for unilateral compensation trimming of the outer surface is formulated, with inner-surface errors as constraints and outer-surface errors as decision variables. Then, the harmonic errors on both surfaces are extracted and 3D-reconstructed using Zernike polynomials and normal cylindrical projection. Finite element simulations confirm that the objective function predictions agree well with simulation results. Finally, a three-axis ion beam global trimming technique is developed that maps the annular error onto a two-dimensional rectangle, performs distortion correction, and solves for the dwell time. Single-pass trimming simultaneously reduced the 1st–4th harmonic errors by over 67.3%, frequency split by 71.2%, and damping asymmetry by 70.7%, while yielding a record-high quality factor of 5.04 × 10⁷. Iterative trimming further validated the proposed relationship models between the objective functions and the dynamic errors. This work provides a deterministic, geometry-driven paradigm that reducing the dependence on repeated performance feedback, enabling efficient manufacturing of navigation-grade resonators.

abstract: This work presents a novel digital image correlation (DIC) framework for full-field measurements of displacement, strain, and damage, based on a phase field (PF) approach. The idea is to take advantage of the ability of the PF method to track complex crack morphologies and to provide a natural way in DIC to perform damage and crack measurements from experimental speckle images, in addition to displacement and strain fields. Moreover, incorporating the damage variable into DIC can improve the displacement accuracy near the crack tip, and can avoid the need of user-defined masks when dealing with cracked samples, which is advantageous when cracks become complex and the manual application of masks becomes challenging. The theoretical formulation of the proposed framework, namely PF-DIC, was presented in detail in the paper, along with a finite element implementation. Numerical examples have demonstrated the capability of the proposed PF-DIC in terms of capturing different types of cracks while providing similar measurement accuracy to that of masked DIC. Additionally, it is shown that the PF-DIC can be easily adapted to selectively identify critical cracks under specific loading conditions or mechanisms for damage assessment and diagnostic purposes. The proposed DIC framework can be used to characterize material defects, support structural health monitoring, and enable a potential unification of PF simulations and experimental fracture measurements

Multi-objective optimization of wellbore-wall insulation parameters for thermal management in ultra-high-temperature wells
abstract: Uncontrolled wellbore temperature in ultra-high-temperature wells is one of the critical engineering bottlenecks restricting the safe and efficient development of unconventional energy resources. As a novel wellbore temperature-control technique, the optimization of engineering parameters for the insulating mud cake (IMC) still lacks systematic theoretical support. In this study, a transient temperature field model in ultra-high-temperature wells under coupled drilling–production conditions is established. By integrating a Gaussian process regression (GPR) surrogate model with the Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm II (NSGA-II), a thermo-economic collaborative optimization of the thermal conductivity (kIMC) and the covered well section length (LIMC) of the IMC is conducted. The results show that wellbore-wall insulation can significantly suppress heat transfer between the wellbore and the formation, extending the thermal equilibrium time under drilling and production conditions to approximately six and five times that of the original conditions, respectively. Under drilling conditions, the bottomhole temperature (BHT) is mainly governed by LIMC; under production conditions, the tubing outlet temperature (TOT) exhibits a markedly amplified high sensitivity to kIMC. Both BHT and TOT display pronounced nonlinear responses to kIMC. When balancing insulation performance and engineering cost, the reasonable range of kIMC is 0.1–0.5 W/(m·℃). The Pareto front obtained from the multi-objective optimization quantitatively reveals the inevitable trade-offs among BHT reduction, TOT enhancement, and cost increase, providing a quantifiable decision-making basis for the engineering selection of wellbore-wall insulation parameters in ultra-high-temperature wells.

title: The interplay between thermomigration and stress-driven hydrogen transport in metals
abstract: Thermomigration is the driving force for hydrogen transport due to a temperature gradient. It can compete with hydrogen transport induced by stress gradients. While stress-driven hydrogen migration is well established, thermomigration remains comparatively underexplored, largely due to limited mechanistic understanding and a scarcity of experimental data. In this work, we develop a thermodynamically consistent framework for hydrogen transport, incorporating a mechanistic model for thermomigration. This is implemented within a finite element framework using an effective chemical potential. Using case studies of iron and nickel heat exchangers and zirconium alloy nuclear fuel cladding, we quantify the competing and synergistic effects of thermomigration and stress-driven transport. We show that thermomigration often dominates hydrogen redistribution in heat-carrying components, even in the presence of significant thermal incompatibility stresses. However, stress-driven transport is shown to become decisive near sharp stress concentrators. A graphical method is introduced to rapidly identify the dominant transport mechanism without requiring fully coupled simulations. The results provide practical guidance for assessing hydrogen redistribution and embrittlement risk in heat-carrying structural components.

title: Plant-inspired programmable stiffness in pressurized cellular solids
abstract: During heatwaves or droughts, soft plant organs wilt by loosing stiffness. This softening corresponds to a loss of intracellular fluid. By controlling osmosis in vitro , the stiffness of soft plant tissues was shown to increase with turgor pressure. This increase was traditionally explained by considering an incompressible fluid enclosed in an elastic membrane and small deformations of the cell walls. However, we found an opposite trend when testing a synthetic cellular tissue. Here we show that the stiffness of pressurized cellular solids depends on the thermodynamic process of the fluid and the hyperelastic behavior of the cell wall. At low pressure, the Young’s modulus of pressurized cellular solids decreases when the pressure inside the cell is fixed (isobaric process). The opposite trend occurs when a liquid is enclosed in the membrane (isochoric process). When pressure is increased, the strain stiffening of the walls dominates and leads to an increase of stiffness regardless of the fluid process. We show that linear elastic models assuming osmotic process are incompatible with turgor-induced stiffening of plants. However, considering nonlinear strain stiffening of cell walls, the observed behavior is recovered. The actual turgor-dependent rigidity of plants may involve more complex mechanisms, possibly combining mechanical, chemical and biological processes. The idealized models of stiffness will be valuable tools for theoretical biology, from plant growth to impacts on soft animal tissues. Furthermore, we believe that the clarification of the fluid–structure interaction in pressurized cellular solids will allow to design active metamaterials with programmable stiffness.

title: Structural design strategies for energy-absorbing auxetic metamaterials: a review
abstract: Auxetic metamaterials exhibit a negative Poisson’s ratio (NPR) through geometry-controlled deformation and offer considerable potential for impact energy absorption. This review systematically examines the structural configurations, deformation mechanisms, enhancement strategies and engineering applications of auxetic energy absorbers. Six representative topology families, including perforated, re-entrant, chiral, rotationally rigid, origami and other specialized structures, are reviewed in terms of their geometry, NPR mechanisms, collapse behavior and energy dissipation performance. Five major enhancement strategies are then evaluated, including baseline enhancement, optimization algorithms, multi-material integration, multi-structure integration and gradient design, with emphasis on their effects on load paths, peak force, plateau stability, densification and failure modes. A distinctive contribution is the quantitative synthesis of 37 paired, within-study comparisons of specific energy absorption (SEA). Reported SEA enhancements range from 6% to 800%, with a median of 81.5%, demonstrating the potential of structural innovation while revealing substantial variability among designs. The analysis indicates that NPR magnitude alone cannot determine energy absorption performance, as geometry, constituent material, relative density, loading conditions, manufacturing precision, environmental conditions and boundary constraints are also critical. Applications in aerospace, transportation, personal protection, biomedical devices and civil infrastructure are reviewed in relation to their functional requirements. Finally, current limitations and future directions are discussed, emphasizing integrated design strategies, manufacturing accuracy, performance under complex loading and environmental conditions, and the transition from laboratory concepts to practical engineering applications.

Phase-synchronized split-type linear piezoelectric actuator
abstract: Friction-driven linear piezoelectric actuators excel in positioning resolution and response speed, yet their speed-thrust-bandwidth performance remains constrained by strongly coupled contact dynamics. This work proposes a split-kinematic linear piezoelectric actuator in which the stator and mover are mechanically separated and independently excited. The architecture introduces the inter-channel phase difference as an additional control variable for synchronizing the normal contact force with the relative tangential velocity. To predict the resulting long-stroke motion, an electromechanical–contact coupled dynamic framework is developed. The framework integrates a simplified transfer-matrix formulation for the distributed vibration field, a Greenwood–Williamson rough-contact model, a regularized friction law, and rigid-body slider dynamics. A dynamic spatial mapping scheme is further introduced to evaluate the local mover vibration velocity at the instantaneous contact coordinate, replacing the conventional uniform-velocity assumption. Experimental vibration measurements show a 39.9% spatial variation of velocity amplitude over the 12 mm stroke, confirming the need for position-dependent mapping. The proposed model predicts transient slider motion with normalized root-mean-square errors below 7% across the tested contact angles and improves prediction accuracy over a spatially averaged baseline under non-uniform vibration conditions. Sensitivity analysis shows that phase difference is the dominant parameter for thrust, whereas speed is governed mainly by the coupled effect of contact angle and phase. The prototype achieves a maximum speed of 580 mm/s, a maximum thrust of 9.6 N, an effective operating bandwidth of 10.5 kHz, and a peak efficiency of 26.0%. The results demonstrate that spatially resolved modeling and phase-synchronized split excitation provide a practical route for improving the controllability and broadband performance of friction-driven linear piezoelectric actuators.

Rapid kirigami simulation using the bar & hinge approach
abstract: Kirigami, the art of cutting sheets, offers unique characteristics such as shape morphing, stretchability, and adaptability, with applications in deployable and reconfigurable structures. While Finite Element (FE) approaches are widely used to analyze kirigami structures, they are computationally intensive and prone to convergence issues. On the other hand, existing simplified and theoretical models for evaluating kirigami are typically restricted to specific designs and analytical scenarios. This paper proposes a generalized, computationally efficient reduced-order model based on the bar and hinge approach for analyzing any kirigami system. The model represents the entire kirigami structure using truss bars, bending hinges, and torsional springs, capturing both the deformation and internal forces of the system. We derive stiffness expressions for kirigami structures that experience stretching and out-of-plane bending deformations, as well as for structures that experience only in-plane stretching and rotations. The accuracy and robustness of the model are validated through comparisons with FE analysis and experimental data on both single-cut kirigami designs and more complex designs with multiple cuts. Our results demonstrate less than 5% difference in deformation predictions and achieve at least a tenfold computational speedup compared to FE simulations. Additionally, we demonstrate the model’s capabilities through simulating complex scenarios, including kirigami-skinned crawlers, high-throughput property-space exploration, and in-plane kirigami-inspired metamaterials. These examples demonstrate computational capabilities that enable large-deformation structural simulations and high-throughput design exploration beyond the practical limits of conventional FE methods.

title: Machine learning-enabled inverse design of heterogeneous impact-resistant metamaterials
abstract: Designing impact-resistant responses in heterogeneous multi-material metamaterials remains challenging because the discrete material-layout space is high-dimensional and non-intuitive, particularly when specific energy absorption (SEA) must be increased without amplifying the peak impact force in applications such as unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) airdrop. Despite recent advances in inverse design, data-driven optimization of impact response remains constrained by the scarcity of high-fidelity datasets that jointly represent dynamic loading and material failure. This study develops a machine-learning-enabled inverse-design framework for non-periodic heterogeneous multi-material metamaterials using a fracture-aware finite-element dataset generated under quasi-static compression and dynamic impact. A ductile damage model is used to represent polylactic acid (PLA) failure, and a Transformer-based surrogate learns the mapping from cell-wise PLA/thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU) layouts to the stress–strain response and peak impact force. The surrogate is coupled with the non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm II (NSGA-II) to identify Pareto-optimal designs in the combinatorial layout space. Across comparable designs, the optimized layouts achieved up to 58% higher SEA and 47.4% lower peak force, and the predicted improvements were verified by quasi-static compression and drop-weight impact tests. In UAV airdrop experiments, the optimized design produced a payload-acceleration peak comparable to that of pure TPU while avoiding the pronounced rebound and overturning observed for the compliant single-material box. These results demonstrate that spatially heterogeneous multi-material layouts can balance energy absorption, force attenuation, and post-impact stability.

title: Editorial Board
Crystal plasticity-guided deep learning for extrapolative prediction of cyclic behaviour
abstract: Quantifying material response under cyclic loading is crucial for fatigue life and structural reliability. Crystal Plasticity Finite Element (CPFE) methods have been widely used to simulate cyclic behaviour. However, such models require careful calibration of numerous parameters, incur substantial computational costs, and exhibit questionable predictability under cyclic loading conditions not used for calibration. Data-driven approaches also suffer from poor extrapolative and predictive capability with limited data. To address these limitations, this study proposes a crystal plasticity-guided deep learning framework combining the physical fidelity of the CPFE model with the efficiency of data-driven methods. This framework consists of a Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG) algorithm and a Transformer model. The approach was guided by crystal plasticity behaviour, using CPFE-simulated stress as both an input to the model and a baseline for predicting experimental cyclic responses. DDPG automatically calibrated the CPFE model parameters over the first three cycles from a 100-cycle cyclic response of 316H stainless steel at a 1.2% strain range (R ratio = -1). Subsequently, Transformer learned the discrepancies between the CPFE and experimental stresses, which were then added to the CPFE-simulated stress to predict experimental cyclic responses. This approach exhibited excellent calibration performance. Furthermore, under various unseen cyclic loading conditions, the framework demonstrated high-fidelity prediction of experimental cyclic behaviour and accurately captured key cyclic deformation characteristics, including the combined isotropic–kinematic hardening and cyclic saturation. It also outperformed the CPFE model in prediction accuracy and a Transformer without crystal-plasticity guidance in extrapolative capability when trained on limited data from initial cycles.

Finite-element-guided inversion network for full-field reconstruction of graded modulus distributions
abstract: Continuous high-throughput mechanical characterization via functionally graded materials (FGMs) enables probing full composition paths in a single specimen, yet full-field reconstruction of continuously varying Young's modulus from displacement measurements remains a high-dimensional, noise-sensitive inverse problem. Conventional adjoint-based iterative methods suffer from high computational cost and sample-specific regularization tuning, while purely data-driven neural networks lack physical consistency and degrade under noisy inputs. This work proposes a finite-element-guided inversion network (FE-GIN) that incorporates weak-form equilibrium information into U-Net training via local and global equilibrium loss formulations. An isoparametric graded finite element formulation is used to generate low-dimensional yet high-fidelity training datasets, enabling efficient learning while preserving the continuous nature of graded modulus fields. Hybrid-loss models are developed to balance reconstruction accuracy and noise robustness. Systematic numerical validation demonstrates that FE-GIN consistently improves noise-free accuracy and markedly enhances noise robustness relative to purely data-driven baselines, with hybrid models achieving optimal accuracy-robustness trade-offs. Compared to adjoint-based benchmarks, FE-GIN outperforms for typical graded patterns, remains competitive for challenging cases and delivers substantial efficiency advantages via single feed-forward inference. These combined strengths support FE-GIN as a promising computational framework for high-throughput mechanical characterization of graded materials.

abstract: Disordered mechanical metamaterials offer advantages over periodic structures, including resistance to localized collapse and reduced anisotropy. Nodal connectivity is a key factor influencing their mechanical behavior, yet how it interacts with structural disorder to affect post-yielding plasticity and anisotropy remains unclear. This study introduces geometric perturbations into hexagonal, square, and triangular metamaterials, generating disorder while preserving nodal connectivity. A dual-uncertainty-aware Gaussian process framework is proposed to capture epistemic and aleatoric uncertainties, achieving R 2 > 0.95 across key compressive properties with at least 80% fewer iterations than baselines. Results show that disorder mitigates both elastic and plastic anisotropy and drives asynchronous collapse to effectively suppress plateau stress oscillations. Meanwhile, nodal connectivity controls the proportion of cell walls that collapse versus those that actively redistribute load, as evidenced by the hexagonal topology sustaining a high plateau stress. These insights provide design guidance for using nodal connectivity to tune disordered metamaterials for load-bearing and energy-absorption applications.
