abstract: Chiral structures have drawn great attention in the engineering community due to their ability to effectively redistribute applied load, thereby exhibiting outstanding mechanical performance. However, their geometry and complicated mechanical responses hinder their efficient design. This work proposes a novel constitutive modeling approach for chiral structures that directly correlates the applied external load with the resulting rotation angle, facilitating the clear identification of the linear elastic response regime. In addition, a chiral structure with hybrid materials is proposed to demonstrate the mechanical performance, such as maximum load capacity and specific elastic energy absorption, based on the proposed constitutive model for chiral structures. Validated by experimental and finite element simulation results, the proposed constitutive modeling method provides new insights for the efficient design of chiral structures.

title: Mobilized friction angle on weak planes under 3D stress states
abstract: Layered rocks may fail either by bedding-parallel sliding along weak planes or by bedding-transverse fracture through the matrix. Classical Jaeger's single-plane-of-weakness theory gives a transparent criterion for this distinction, but it is restricted to conventional triaxial stress states and does not include the independent role of the intermediate principal stress. This study extends the weak-plane formulation to general three-dimensional stress states by parameterizing the stress tensor with mean stress, deviatoric stress intensity and generalized Lode angle. Closed-form expressions are derived for the normal and shear stresses on a weak plane, and the resulting Mohr-circle family is shown to satisfy an elliptical constraint. The mobilized friction angle is then used as a failure-mode indicator. Tangent-line geometry gives its global maximum in closed form, showing that the upper bound depends only on stress triaxiality and not on Lode angle or weak-plane dip. This result further yields a dimensionless sufficient condition under which bedding-parallel sliding is excluded for all orientations. Parametric maps show that Lode angle can change the peak mobilized friction angle from 15.4° to 46.2° at a stress triaxiality of 0.8, whereas the conventional Jaeger angles give an intermediate value of 31.1°. The criterion predicts the initial stability and injection-fault slip onset in the Mont Terri fluid-injection experiment and agrees with 3DEC true-triaxial simulations within the 10° Lode-angle resolution. The formulation provides a compact analytical basis for failure-mode mapping in layered rocks under three-dimensional stress states.

title: Experimental realization of perfect absorption in non-Hermitian piezoelectric metagratings
Twisting Kelvin cells for enhanced vibration control
abstract: This study introduces a minimalist design strategy to engineer wave propagation in cellular metamaterials by applying a single-parameter twist to the classical Kelvin unit cell. By breaking the cell’s symmetry while preserving its lattice topology, this geometric modification activates and tunes band-gap frequencies with up to a 9% mass increase, without introducing explicit inertial elements or added geometric complexity, enabling wave-filtering behavior absent in the untwisted reference configuration. The proposed strategy employs complex-valued Bloch–Floquet analysis of quasi-one-dimensional periodic chains, revealing symmetry-breaking triggers that activate two distinct wave-attenuation mechanisms: a complete Bragg-type and a polarization-dependent band gap arising from longitudinal–torsional mode coupling, both narrow but induced with negligible mass increment. These findings are substantiated by a physics-driven analytical model that captures the mode-coupling-induced avoided crossings and provides key insight into the wave characteristics of twisted Kelvin-cell architectures. Transmission measurements on SLA-printed three-cell specimens validate the predictive fidelity of this approach, revealing up to 20 dB of wave attenuation. We show that accounting for material viscoelasticity is essential for accurate prediction, as idealized linear-elastic models cannot capture band-gap frequencies in polymer-based chains. Overall, we show that modest, well-defined modifications to a classical parent geometry yield tunable, mass-efficient wave-filtering performance. This offers a tractable design strategy for vibration control in lightweight lattices.

abstract: ABSTRACT With the rapid development of nanotechnologies, silicon carbide (SiC) nanostructures have been widely adopted in a broad range of cutting-edge applications as their basic building blocks. To ensure the service reliability of those intelligent devices, an in-depth understanding of their mechanical properties is crucial given that most of the dysfunction of those devices are directly caused by the mechanical failure of their basic units. Due to the ‘size effect’, materials’ properties undergo significant alterations when shrunk down to the micro-/nanoscale, which distinguishes them from their bulk counterparts. Thus, a comprehensive understanding of one-dimensional (1D) semiconductor nanocrystals’ mechanical properties is also crucial for the design, fabrication, and application of SiC-based devices. In this study, by employing a quantitative in situ measurement strategy, the mechanical properties of three classical types of SiC (3C-, 6H-, and 4H-) micro-/nanocrystals were investigated inside electron microscopes. Results demonstrated that all the three SiC polytypes exhibited ‘small is stronger’ size-dependent fracture strengths. Surprisingly, all these covalently-bonded SiC nanocrystals exhibited exceptionally large deformation behaviors with maximum strains exceeding 10% before rupturing in typical brittle fashions. Molecular dynamics simulations qualitatively indicated the elastic–brittle nature of SiC under tensile loading and further suggested a surface-dominated inverse size effect at ultrasmall scales, as well as a size- and condition-dependent change in the failure mode under compressive loading. Considering the potential breakthrough in intrinsic properties of covalent crystals brought about by their subtle strain tunability, we anticipate that the performance of covalent nanomaterials will usher in significant advancements under ultra-large strains.

Multi-parameter analysis of compliant impact oscillator with time-delayed feedback control
abstract: Engineering impact systems often involve the combined effects of compliant contacts and time delays, whose interaction can generate complex nonlinear dynamics that are difficult to predict using conventional local analysis. This study investigates the global dynamics and control of a harmonically excited compliant impact oscillator, a canonical model representative of a wide class of vibro-impact mechanical systems. Mapping of the excitation-parameter plane identifies periodic, quasi-periodic and chaotic responses, together with multistability over substantial parameter regions. In particular, parameter regions are identified where up to four distinct periodic attractors coexist, with intricate basin structures governing the final system response. To suppress undesirable oscillatory regimes, a velocity-based time-delayed feedback controller is introduced. Control design maps are constructed to delineate regions of stable operation in the control parameter space, providing practical guidance for selecting controller parameters to achieve robust periodic motion. Further analysis shows that the fundamental periodic solutions evolve through grazing, period-doubling, saddle–node and Hopf bifurcations, revealing the mechanisms responsible for stability transitions in the system. The results clarify how compliant impacts and delayed feedback interact to shape the global stability and multistability of impact oscillators, offering insights relevant to the design and control of vibro-impact devices, while serving as a theoretical baseline for understanding more complex physical systems.

abstract: Impact performance of lightweight lattice structures depends on both material properties and architectural topology, especially under localized versus global loading. This work examines the low-speed impact response of additively manufactured AlSi10Mg triply periodic minimal surface (TPMS) lattices through combined experimental and numerical methods. Nine sheet-based topologies at 25% relative density are tested under localized penetration (100–300 J), followed by crushing of four topologies across 15–25% relative density (20–60 J), with force-displacement response, deformation mechanics, and energy absorption systematically quantified. Diamond shows the highest penetration resistance (∼18.8 mm at 300 J), while Lidinoid shows the lowest, with full perforation already at 200 J. Finite element models incorporating calibrated Johnson-Cook plasticity and damage show good predictive capability for the Diamond and Gyroid topologies across all tested energies, and for all four topologies at 100 J, reproducing initial stiffness, crater formation, and force-penetration trends, with peak-force errors generally within 10%. Predictive accuracy decreases at higher energies and for the junction-dominated I-WP and Primitive topologies, where peak-force errors reach up to 44.7%, reflecting the framework's limits under unresolved manufacturing defects and discrete fracture. Topology exerts a first-order influence on impact response, supporting topology-specific selection of TPMS lattices for lightweight impact mitigation.

abstract: Traditional particle-reinforced composite materials face several challenges such as particle agglomeration, poor interfacial load transfer that can lead to premature failure, manufacturing complexities, and increased weight. Motivated by these limitations, this work designs, additively manufactures, and tests new classes of periodic and aperiodic particle-reinforced composite-like metamaterials (PRCM). Unlike conventional particle-reinforced composites, the mechanical performance of the proposed PRCM is governed by the synergistic interplay between the lattice topology that replaces the dense matrix and inclusion, and the geometry and spatial distribution of the particles, thereby extending the design space beyond that achievable through conventional rule-of-mixtures approaches. Guided by the composite rule of mixtures, the effect of inclusion volume fraction (16% - 33%), relative density (40%, 50%, and 60%), and geometry (spherical, cubic, and cylindrical), while maintaining the latticed matrix relative density at 20%, was investigated. Numerical simulations using periodic boundary conditions showed that the PRCMs distributed stresses over a larger volume than the unreinforced lattice, resulting in improved resistance under uniaxial and shear loading. Compression tests revealed localized plastic deformation around the particles, leading to earlier yielding. However, reducing the spacing between particles promoted crack bridging and improved load transfer. Without increasing weight, the metamaterial with periodically distributed spherical inclusions exhibited a 122% increase in peak compressive strength and a 27% increase in toughness compared to the unreinforced metamaterial. In flexure, the discrete latticed particle reinforcement strategy was not effective, as cracks preferentially propagated through particle-deficient regions. However, aligning latticed fibers along the span of a three-point bending latticed beam in a periodic body-centered cubic arrangement increased the specific flexural peak load and toughness by 33% and 59%, respectively. Overall, these results demonstrate that PRCMs provide a practical approach for improving the strength, toughness, and stiffness of lightweight metamaterials subjected to compressive and bending loads while overcoming several limitations associated with traditional PRC.

Microstructure-informed ICME framework for laser-assisted flange forming of S700 steel
abstract: In multi-step sheet metal forming, the deformation and damage state inherited from upstream operations can govern failure during subsequent processing. Conventional process-chain simulations commonly transfer macroscopic quantities such as equivalent plastic strain, which do not uniquely represent the underlying microstructural state. This work presents an Integrated Computational Materials Engineering (ICME) framework for laser-assisted flange forming of S700MC steel, sequentially coupling shear cutting, localized laser heating, and flange forming through deterministic transfer of dislocation densities and void fraction as microstructural state variables (MSV) using a damage-integrated thermo-micro-mechanical (D-TMM) formulation. A circumferential binning procedure is introduced to quantify spatial variations of each field along the flange edge. The simulations reveal persistent damage localization near 35° and 70°, robust to circumferential discretization, evaluation-region height, and removal of one symmetry plane. A conventional formulation transferring equivalent plastic strain and void fraction predicts higher mean plastic strain but does not reproduce this localization. D-TMM control simulations show that the shear-sensitive damage contribution is required for the angular damage pattern, while transferred MSVs increase its severity. Increasing the forming-zone temperature from approximately 350°C to 550°C reduces numerical fracture by about 72%, while blank inversion yields an overall reduction of about 85% relative to the 350°C condition. Representative experiments support the predicted response through forming-force and flange-thickness comparisons. The mean grain aspect ratio decreases from 4.55 to 2.47 from cold to laser-assisted forming, while simulated wall-immobile dislocation densities are of the same order of magnitude as EBSD-derived GND densities, differing by approximately a factor of 1.4. The framework therefore provides a microstructure-informed basis for assessing edge fracture in sequential forming processes.

title: Lightweight brain-coral-inspired aperiodic lattices with tailored strength and energy absorption
abstract: Periodic cellular architectures can undergo coordinated buckling, making stable collapse challenging in lightweight structures requiring both high collapse resistance and energy absorption. Here, we introduce brain-coral-inspired aperiodic lattices generated from Gray–Scott reaction–diffusion patterns. Smooth-walled prismatic lattices with controlled relative density were fabricated by masked stereolithography and evaluated under quasi-static out-of-plane compression using experiments and finite element simulations. At 30% nominal relative density, the baseline coral-inspired lattice achieved an initial collapse stress of 5.8 MPa, 81% and 36% higher than those of the hexagonal and triangular honeycombs, respectively. This collapse-strength advantage did not translate into the highest specific energy absorption among the reference lattices. Intermediate panels had limited influence on collapse strength but compartmentalized deformation. Consequently, specific energy absorption (SEA) increased from approximately 1.8 J/g to over 6 J/g in three- and four-panel configurations, with the four-panel lattice outperforming all tested references in SEA. Plastic-strain and plastic-dissipation fields showed that the panels distributed crushing across multiple compartments, supporting the distinct roles of wall morphology and segmentation. Design-space exploration identified architectures with greater collapse resistance, which was linked most strongly to closed-pore area fraction and junction density. With four panels, the best-performing architecture achieved a specific strength of 17.5 MPa cm 3 /g and specific energy absorption of 10.45 J/g. Contextual benchmarking placed the selected architectures in a region of high normalised specific strength and energy absorption. These findings establish Gray–Scott-generated morphology and structural segmentation as complementary design variables for tailoring collapse initiation and post-collapse energy absorption.

abstract: Resolving the spatiotemporal evolution of fracture processes in brittle materials under extreme loading remains a fundamental challenge. Conventional acoustic-emission-based approaches are often limited by overlapping signals during rapid crack propagation and by strongly distorted wave paths caused by material heterogeneity. In this study, we introduce a fracture-surface-constrained AE reconstruction framework that links calibrated acoustic waveforms with high-resolution post-mortem fracture-surface measurements. The novelty of the method is that AE source locations are not inferred from waveforms alone; instead, waveform-derived occurrence time and corner frequency are constrained by the measured fracture geometry, displacement discontinuity, and surface-derived seismic moment. This enables spatially distributed AE source events, source-radius evolution, and near-simultaneous fracture activity to be reconstructed under high-rate loading conditions where conventional arrival-time-based localization becomes difficult. The proposed framework therefore provides a new route for reconstructing dynamic fracture processes in brittle materials by combining acoustic radiation with direct fracture-surface evidence, rather than relying solely on waveform-based source localization.

A unified strain energy decomposition framework for phase-field fracture modelling
abstract: In the phase-field modelling framework, strain energy is commonly decomposed into positive and negative components to capture the tension–compression asymmetry of materials. Nevertheless, most existing decomposition strategies are valid only for specific stress-state cases, limiting their applicability in simulating fracture propagation in real-world structures that often experience complex and varying stress conditions. To overcome this limitation, a unified strain energy decomposition framework applicable to arbitrary stress states is proposed. Within this framework, the elastic strain energy is divided into three non-negative components, namely tensile, shear and compressive strain energy. A local coordinate system is determined by maximising the F -function energy dissipation, which drives the damage evolution. Depending on the ratio of shear to tensile fracture toughness and the value of Poisson’s ratio, the proposed unified framework can degenerate into existing decomposition schemes such as the spectral, volumetric–deviatoric (V–D), or crack-direction-based decomposition methods under specific stress states. The unified phase-field model, implemented in ABAQUS platform through the VUEL and VUMAT subroutines, was verified via a single-element benchmark and subsequently validated through a series of numerical examples under tensile, compressive, and shear stress states. Those results illustrated that the proposed energy decomposition framework consistently reproduces fracture evolution across arbitrary stress states, showing superior generality, robustness, and accuracy compared with currently existing decomposition approaches.

abstract: The dynamic performance of cutting tools is a critical factor governing stability, surface quality, and productivity in machining processes. However, the development of dynamically optimized cutting tools remains a major multidisciplinary challenge due to the lack of design methodologies. This challenge is particularly critical for large cutting tools customized for specific applications, whose high mass, low specific stiffness, and low natural frequencies make them especially susceptible to chatter, thereby limiting machining performance. This work proposes a unified methodology for the dynamic optimization of cutting tools by integrating Topology Optimization (TO), multiscale Finite Element Method (FEM), and Additive Manufacturing (AM). The main novelty lies in the development and integration of predictive modeling, optimization, and manufacturing approaches into a unified methodology, with original contributions in each domain. A new multiscale FEM strategy couples meso-scale cutting force prediction with macro-scale static and dynamic simulations, incorporating machine-tool spindle effects into the dynamic analysis. This enables cutting forces to be incorporated into both topology optimization and structural validation. TO is employed to satisfy target mass, stiffness, and natural frequency requirements, while hybrid AM enables the fabrication of complex geometries with high accuracy. In addition, internal coolant channels are optimized through Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD). The methodology is demonstrated in an industrially relevant case study involving a large customized cutting tool for e-mobility. Experimental modal analysis and machining tests validate the predictive models and the performance of the optimized tool, demonstrating 50% productivity improvement while improving surface roughness compared with the industrial benchmark design.

title: Feedstock Morphology Governs Impact-Induced Deformation in Cold Sprayed Metal-Ceramic Composites
abstract: The mechanistic understanding of cold spray additive manufacturing for metal-ceramic composites has mainly focused on spray parameters, whereas the role of metallic feedstock morphology remains comparatively underexplored. This study elucidates how spherical and spongy Cu morphologies govern impact-induced deformation, microstructural evolution, and the resulting structure-property relationship in Cu-Al 2 O 3 composite deposits. Multi-scale characterization, including microstructural analysis, nano- and micro-hardness measurements, micro-compression tests, and tribological analyses, reveals distinct strain patterns within the deposits that are influenced by particle morphology. Spherical Cu promotes interfacial strain localization and interfacial metal–ceramic contacts along flattened splats, giving rise to a distinct bimodal grain structure characterized by grain refinement at splat boundaries and larger, unrefined grains within splat cores. This microstructural gradient effectively balances strength and ductility. In contrast, the collapse of the spongy Cu ligament upon impact forms a volumetrically distributed strain-hardened zone, resulting in a more broadly distributed strain accumulation and enhanced ceramic encapsulation. The findings indicate that ceramic particles play an active role in influencing deformation caused by impact, while also passively strengthening the deposits. This dual function is directly reflected in the enhanced performance of the deposits, even at comparable reinforcement fraction. These findings demonstrate that, in addition to the spray parameters, the powder morphology serves as a fundamental governing factor in controlling the deformation mechanisms and deposit performance.
